derivations.claim: Fix one state $s$. Write $\Delta_a=q_s(a)-p_s(a)$; since both distributions have mass one, $\sum_a\Delta_a=0$. The set $B=\{a:\Delta_a\ge0\}$ consists of the nonnegative differences. The positive and negative parts of $\Delta$ therefore have equal sum, each equal to $\frac12\sum_a|\Delta_a|$. For every subset $C\subseteq A(s)$, $|\sum_{a\in C}\Delta_a|$ is at most this common sum, and $C=B$ attains it. Thus the event-supremum total variation in [F2] equals $\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)$.

Apply [F3] to the probability measures $q_s$ and $p_s$ on the finite power-set space, and use step 1.1. This gives $\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)\le\sqrt{D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)/2}$, including the infinite-divergence case.

If $K=+\infty$, the asserted inequality holds because each total-variation term is at most one. Suppose $K<\infty$ and put $m=K/2$. When $m=0$, step 2.1 gives $D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)\ge2\operatorname{TV}_{A(s)}(q_s,p_s)^2\ge0$ for every state. Since their $d$-weighted sum is zero, every state with $d(s)>0$ has zero divergence, so step 2.1 also gives zero total variation there. When $m>0$, for every $x\ge0$ the square $(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt m)^2\ge0$ gives $\sqrt{x}\le(\sqrt m+x/\sqrt m)/2$. Apply this with $x=D_{\rm KL}(q_s\|p_s)/2$ for states with $d(s)>0$, multiply by $d(s)$, and sum. Since $\sum_sd(s)=1$ and $\sum_sd(s)x_s=m$, the result is $\sum_sd(s)\sqrt{x_s}\le\sqrt m$. Step 2.1 now yields the claimed bound.

Every partial sum and the limit satisfy
Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

derivations.claim: The initial vector $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ is nonnegative and sums to one. If $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution, then the recurrence and [F2]–[F3] give nonnegative next masses and $\sum_{s'}\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s')=\sum_s\sum_{a\in A(s)}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)\sum_{s',\rho}p(s',\rho\mid s,a)=\sum_s\mu_t^\pi(s)=1$. By [F8], every $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution.

By [F4] and step 1.1, $d^\pi(s)\ge0$ and $\sum_s d^\pi(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_s\mu_t^\pi(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t=1$ by [F6]. Interchanging the finite state sum with the nonnegative series is valid because $S$ is finite. Thus $d^\pi$ is a probability distribution.

For each $t$, the finite transition weights $\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)$ are nonnegative and sum to one by step 1.1 and [F2]–[F3]. Hence their weighted sum of $g$ has absolute value at most $B$. Apply [F7] to this bounded sequence of time-$t$ signal sums; the series in [F5] converges absolutely and its absolute value is at most $B/(1-\gamma)$.

derivations.claim: For $\sigma\in\{\pi,\pi'\}$, every entry of $K_\sigma$ is nonnegative and each column sums to one by [F1]. Thus $K_\sigma^t$ is column-stochastic for every $t$, and its induced matrix $1$-norm $\|A\|_1:=\max_s\sum_{s'}|A(s',s)|$ is one. The matrix series $G_\sigma:=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^tK_\sigma^t$ converges in this norm by [F4]; its finite partial sums satisfy $(I-\gamma K_\sigma)\sum_{t=0}^{N}\gamma^tK_\sigma^t=I-\gamma^{N+1}K_\sigma^{N+1}$, whose remainder norm tends to zero by [F5]. The same identity with multiplication on the other side shows $G_\sigma=(I-\gamma K_\sigma)^{-1}$.

By [F1], for each coordinate $s'$ of $(K_{\pi'}-K_\pi)d^\pi$, the triangle inequality gives $\sum_{s'}|((K_{\pi'}-K_\pi)d^\pi)(s')|\le\sum_{s,a,s'}d^\pi(s)|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|P(s'\mid s,a)=2\sum_s d^\pi(s)\operatorname{TV}_s(\pi',\pi)$, because $\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)=1$.

The recurrence in [F1] and the matrix definition in [F2] give $\mu_t^\sigma=K_\sigma^t\mu$, hence $d^\sigma=(1-\gamma)G_\sigma\mu$. The inverse identity $G_{\pi'}-G_\pi=G_{\pi'}[(I-\gamma K_\pi)-(I-\gamma K_{\pi'})]G_\pi$ therefore yields $d^{\pi'}-d^\pi=\gamma G_{\pi'}(K_{\pi'}-K_\pi)d^\pi$.
Since $\|G_{\pi'}\|_1\le\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^t=1/(1-\gamma)$ by [F4] and column-stochasticity, combine step 2.1 with step 1.2 to obtain the claimed $1$-norm bound.

derivations.claim: Fix a policy $\sigma$. For each $t$, let $e_t^\sigma$ be the finite transition-mass sum of $g$ at time $t$, and let $h_t^\sigma:=\sum_s\mu_t^\sigma(s)f(s)$. By [F1] and the definition of $\delta_f^g$, the finite sum of $\delta_f^g$ at time $t$ is $e_t^\sigma+\gamma h_{t+1}^\sigma-h_t^\sigma$. Summing after multiplication by $\gamma^t$ for $t=0,\ldots,N$ telescopes to $\sum_{t=0}^N\gamma^t e_t^\sigma-h_0^\sigma+\gamma^{N+1}h_{N+1}^\sigma$.

The remainder satisfies $|\gamma^{N+1}h_{N+1}^\sigma|\le\gamma^{N+1}\|f\|_\infty\to0$ by [F4] and [F5]. Also $|\delta_f^g|\le\|g\|_\infty+(1+\gamma)\|f\|_\infty$, so [F4] makes its discounted series convergent. Passing to the limit in step 1.1 and using [F2]–[F3] gives $J_g^\sigma(\mu)=\sum_s\mu(s)f(s)+(1-\gamma)^{-1}\sum_s d^\sigma(s)\bar\delta_f^{g,\sigma}(s)$.

Apply the identity in step 2.1 to $\sigma=\pi'$ and $\sigma=\pi$ and subtract; the initial terms $\sum_s\mu(s)f(s)$ cancel. Add and subtract $\sum_s d^\pi(s)\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$. The first resulting term is $L_{\pi,f}^g(\pi')$ by its definition, and the second is $\sum_s(d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s))\bar\delta_f^{g,\pi'}(s)$. Dividing by $1-\gamma>0$ gives the claimed identity.

citations.quote:
Let $M=(S,\mathcal R,(A(s))_{s\in S},p)$ be a finite Markov decision process with nonempty state set $S$ and finite nonempty action set $A(s)$ at each state. Put $\mathcal X=\{(s,a,\rho,s'):s\in S,\ a\in A(s),\ \rho\in\mathcal R,\ s'\in S\}$. Let $\mu$ be a probability distribution on $S$, let $\gamma\in[0,1)$, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and for each $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $b_i\in\mathbb R$, $C_i\ge0$, and $c_i:\mathcal X\to[-C_i,C_i]$. A **finite discounted constrained Markov decision process (CMDP)** is the tuple consisting of $M$, $\mu$, $\gamma$, and the bounded transition-cost functions and thresholds $(c_i,b_i)_{i=1}^m$. Its immediate reward signal is $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$.

For a stationary Markov policy $\pi$, define the state-mass sequence recursively by $\mu_0^\pi=\mu$ and

$$\mu_{t+1}^\pi(s'):=\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a).$$

This recurrence defines nonnegative finite-time masses; the result that each $\mu_t^\pi$ is a probability distribution is established separately.

Let a finite discounted CMDP and a stationary policy $\pi$ be given. The **column transition matrix** $K_\pi$ has entry

$$K_\pi(s',s):=\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a),$$

so that its column indexed by $s$ gives the next-state distribution from current state $s$. With the state-mass column vectors $\mu_t^\pi$ from the CMDP definition, the **normalized discounted state occupancy** is

$$d^\pi(s):=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\mu_t^\pi(s).$$

This normalization is part of the definition; the occupancy is a probability distribution by the separate well-definedness result below.

Let a finite discounted CMDP have initial distribution $\mu$, discount $\gamma\in[0,1)$, $m$ bounded transition signals $c_i$, thresholds $b_i$, and finite-time state masses $\mu_t^\pi$ under a stationary policy $\pi$, as defined in the CMDP model. For any bounded transition signal $g$ on $(s,a,\rho,s')$, define its **expected discounted sum** under $\pi$ by

$$J_g^\pi(\mu):=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{a\in A(s)}\sum_{\rho\in\mathcal R}\sum_{s'\in S}\mu_t^\pi(s)\pi(a\mid s)p(s',\rho\mid s,a)g(s,a,\rho,s').$$

The expected discounted reward is $J^\pi:=J_r^\pi(\mu)$ for the immediate reward signal $r(s,a,\rho,s')=\rho$, and the $i$th expected discounted cost is $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)$. The policy $\pi$ is **feasible** for the discounted-cost constraints exactly when $J_{c_i}^\pi(\mu)\le b_i$ for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Feasibility constrains these expectations; it does not assert a per-trajectory bound.

derivations.claim: The deterministic transition and policy masses are normalized, and both the reward and cost are bounded, so this is a finite CMDP. By [F2] its occupancy has $d^\pi(s)=d^{\pi'}(s)=1$ at $\gamma=0$. By [F3] both reward returns equal $1$, and thus $J(\pi')-J(\pi)=0$.

Since $f=0$ and the reward is $1$, the residual is $\delta_f=1$ and $\epsilon_f=1$. The stated surrogate is $L_{\pi,f}(\pi')=1$. Identical policies have statewise total variation zero, so $D^-_{\pi,f}(\pi')=D^+_{\pi,f}(\pi')=1$. The asserted lower inequality is $1\le0$, which is false by step 1.1. Subtracting the old-policy residual expectation instead gives the corrected surrogate $1-1=0$.
